description: "A computer vision task that locates objects in an image or video frame and predicts a class for each one."
term: "Object Detection"

## Simple explanation

Object detection answers two questions about an image: what objects are
present, and where are they? A detector commonly returns a class label, a
confidence score, and a bounding box for each detected object.

## Technical explanation

Object detection is a structured prediction task. A model predicts one or
more regions, their classes, and confidence values. Common approaches
include two-stage detectors that propose regions before classification and
localization, and single-stage detectors that predict boxes and classes
more directly.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Detection supports applications such as inventory counting, robotics, and
traffic analysis. Evaluation must account for both classification and
localization, often using intersection over union and average precision.
Real deployments also need to consider speed, camera variation, and
consequences of missed or false detections.

## How it works

The image is encoded into visual features. Detection heads use those
features to predict candidate boxes and class scores. A post-processing
step such as [Non-Maximum Suppression (NMS)](../N/non-maximum-suppression-nms.qmd)
may remove duplicate boxes.

## Practical example

A warehouse camera system could detect boxes on a conveyor and return a
bounding box and class for each visible package. Engineers would test it
across different lighting, camera angles, package types, and occlusions.

## Common misconceptions

- Object detection is different from image classification, which typically assigns labels to an entire image without locating instances.
- A confidence score is not automatically a calibrated probability.
- A correct class with an inaccurate box may still count as an incorrect detection under the evaluation rule.
